Week 4: frailty index and CBC-derived inflammatory markers

Reproduction of Han et al., BMC Public Health 2024;24:3408 (NHANES 1999-2016)

  • 1. Summary
  • 2. Verification
  • 3. Data
  • 4. Group comparisons
  • 5. Trend tests and comparison with Tables 2 and 3
  • 6. An AI error that changed results

1. Summary

Of 239 reported numbers, 37 match within rounding, 56 differ for an identified reason (53 because our analytic sample differs, 3 paper typos) and 146 differ without a proven cause. Our analytic sample has N = 14054 against the paper’s 13,507, and the counts already differ at the first exclusion step (24119 aged 50+ in the downloaded files against the paper’s 21,670; no age or exam-status rule reproduces 21,670). Marker distributions agree closely (Table 1 total NLR median 2.14 vs 2.14; our sample quartile cut-offs are within 1.5% of the printed ones). The frailty index does not: weighted frail prevalence is 18.7% in our build and 19.0% in an independent build written without access to ours (FI r = 0.9994), against the paper’s 24%, so every odds ratio and event count sits below the paper’s and stays open. Two unstated choices in the paper were identified from the numbers: Table 2 odds ratios are per log10 unit (per-ln odds ratios match no cell), and the models are survey-weighted (confidence-interval widths match the weighted fit, not the unweighted one). With both, Table 3 top-quartile odds ratios (Model 2) are 0.06-0.08 below the paper’s with overlapping intervals and the same direction; every P for trend is below 0.001 except SII in Model 2 (0.0037). The week’s two verification checks pass: simulated FWER agrees with 1 - 0.95^k within Monte Carlo error, and null p-values are uniform except Kruskal-Wallis at n = 10 per group, whose chi-square approximation is conservative.

4. Group comparisons

FI across quartiles of each marker (our sample quartiles), N = 14054, unweighted.

Boxplots

Residual diagnostics

No normality test is used: at N ≈ 14,000 any test rejects trivial departures. The plots show right-skewed residuals (skewness ≈ 0.8) with a floor at FI = 0; with about 3,500 per group the group means are close to normal regardless.

6. An AI error that changed results

What. In the first version of the data build (written by the nhanes-data-builder agent), the frailty-index item “healthcare use: 10 or more visits in the past year” was scored as code ≥ 6 in every cycle. That cut-off is right for HUQ051 (2013-2016, codes 0-8), but HUQ050 (1999-2012) has only codes 0-5 (4 = 10-12 visits, 5 = 13 or more). The deficit could therefore never be scored for anyone in 1999-2012, silently lowering the frailty index for 7 of 9 cycles.

How it was caught. The ai-error-auditor agent checked each FI item’s code against the NHANES codebooks and found zero people aged 50+ with HUQ050 codes 6-8 in any 1999-2012 cycle. The coordinator confirmed it in the raw files (HUQ050 values 0-5 plus 77/99 only) before the fix, and a second audit verified the fix against an independent rebuild of all 36 items (0 mismatches).

Before and after. R/09 re-runs the final FI code with only this cut-off reverted, so the difference below is this error alone (same analytic sample).

version analytic N healthcare deficit, 1999-2012 (%) healthcare deficit, 2013-2016 (%) mean FI frail n frail % (unweighted) frail % (weighted)
before fix (HUQ050 >= 6) 14054 0.00 18.02 0.1931 2848 20.26 17.67 (SE 0.47)
after fix (HUQ050 >= 4) 14054 20.52 18.02 0.1976 3021 21.50 18.73 (SE 0.47)

The fix moved 173 people above FI = 0.3 and raised the weighted prevalence by 1.06 percentage points, closing 17% of the gap to the paper’s 24%.
